questions.question: What is the difference between a byte and a rune in Go?
questions.title: Rune Vs Byte
questions.direct_answer: A byte (uint8) = one raw memory byte. A rune (int32) = one Unicode code point. ASCII: 1 byte = 1 rune. Beyond ASCII (é, emoji): one rune encodes as MULTIPLE bytes — len(s) counts bytes, utf8.RuneCountInString(s) counts runes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Rune Vs Byte beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: A byte (uint8) = one raw memory byte. A rune (int32) = one Unicode code point. ASCII: 1 byte = 1 rune. Beyond ASCII (é, emoji): one rune encodes as.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A byte is Go's smallest integer (uint8 — one raw byte). A rune is Go's Unicode code point (int32). In strings they compose via UTF-8: a string is a byte sequence where each rune is 1-4 bytes.

The numbers, executed:

```go
s := "héllo"
len(s)                    // 6 — BYTES (h, é=2 bytes, l, l, o)
utf8.RuneCountInString(s) // 5 — RUNES
s[1]                      // 195 — first byte of é's 2-byte encoding
[]rune(s)[1]              // 233 — the rune é itself
```

ASCII hides the difference (1 byte = 1 rune); anything international breaks the naive assumption. s[i] is a byte value; []rune(s)[i] is a code point (after an O(n) conversion — the cost).

The iteration distinction: for i, r := range s yields RUNES with BYTE-offset indices — i jumps by encoding width. Executed: héllo gives i=0 (h), i=1 (é), then i=3 (l — é occupied 2 bytes). A raw loop over len(s) sees meaningless half-rune values at é's position.

The mistake this catches: len(s) as 'character count.' It's byte count. Character count is utf8.RuneCountInString — or don't count: range already yields each rune once.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[helo - 6 bytes] --> B[s1=195 byte fragment]
    S --> R[rune s1=233 - the rune e]
    LEN[len=6 bytes] --- RC[RuneCount=5 runes]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The UTF-8 encoding behind every fact here: code points 0-127 encode as 1 byte (ASCII). 128-2047 as 2. 2048-65535 as 3 (most CJK). 65536+ as 4 (emoji). The first byte's high bits announce the width (0xxxxxxx = 1 byte; 110xxxxx = 2; 1110xxxx = 3; 11110xxx = 4) — how range decodes without lookups, and why a mid-rune byte can never look like a start.

The rune type's identity: rune IS int32 — an alias, not a distinct type. It exists as documentation: 'this int32 means a code point.' byte IS uint8 — same relationship. The types are vocabulary; the semantics are UTF-8's.

Why not a fixed-width 'char' like Java's UTF-16: UTF-8 is the network/file format already (zero conversion at IO boundaries); ASCII (the common case) pays 1 byte/char instead of 2 or 4; the variable-width cost is confined to code that needs character logic (range, []rune, utf8) while byte-oriented code pays nothing. The trade: make Unicode explicit over making everything pay for it.

questions.question: How does Go iterate over strings — bytes or runes?
questions.title: When would you use Rune Vs Byte in a real project
questions.direct_answer: range iterates RUNES (value is a code point, index is a BYTE OFFSET). Indexing s[i] gives BYTES. For byte iteration: classic loop over len(s), or range []byte(s).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Rune Vs Byte.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: range iterates RUNES (value is a code point, index is a BYTE OFFSET).

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The default is runes, with byte-offset indices — the surprising part:

```go
s := "héllo"
for i, r := range s {
    fmt.Println(i, r)   // 0 104 | 1 233 | 3 108 | 4 108 | 5 111
}
```

Executed: i starts 0 (h), then 1 (é — rune 233 at byte offset 1), then JUMPS to 3 (l — é was 2 bytes wide). Index = byte offset; value = decoded rune. range walks UTF-8, not bytes.

Why byte offsets: slicing composes — s[i:] needs byte offsets, and range's i is exactly where each rune starts. Building substrings from iteration output is direct.

Explicit byte iteration, when you want the raw encoding:

```go
for i := 0; i < len(s); i++ {
    b := s[i]     // 104, 195, 169, 108...
}
```

No offset jumps here — i advances by 1 — but values at multi-byte positions are encoding fragments, not characters.

The reversed mistake: []rune(s) in a loop (O(n) allocation per conversion) when range decodes for free. Convert only for random rune access or mutation.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    LOOP[for i, r := range s] --> DEC[decode rune at i]
    DEC --> Y[yield i, r]
    Y --> ADV[i += rune width 1-4]
    ADV --> DEC
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The decoder behind range: each iteration reads the current byte, infers width from leading bits (UTF-8 is self-synchronizing forward), gathers that many bytes, decodes, returns (offset, rune). O(n) total, O(1) per rune, no allocation — decoding happens in registers.

Why byte-offset (not rune-index) for the loop's first value: s[start:end] needs byte offsets, and range's i gives exactly where each rune starts — substring building from iteration is direct. A rune-index loop can't slice without recomputing offsets.

The invalid-UTF-8 case: a Go string CAN hold arbitrary bytes (strings are byte sequences, not guaranteed UTF-8). range handles invalid sequences by yielding U+FFFD (replacement character) with width 1 — no panic, no stop; each invalid byte becomes one replacement rune. That makes range safe over ANY string — and explains why byte loops and rune loops can disagree on corrupt input's count.

questions.question: Why does indexing a string return a byte, not a character?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Rune Vs Byte
questions.direct_answer: s[i] is the i-th BYTE of the UTF-8 encoding (uint8). Characters are variable width — no O(1) 'character at index' exists in UTF-8. The language gives you the byte honestly; runes are opt-in ([]rune, range, utf8).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Rune Vs Byte.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: s[i] is the i-th BYTE of the UTF-8 encoding (uint8). Characters are variable width — no O(1) 'character at index' exists in UTF-8. The language gives you the byte honestly.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Indexing is bytes because that's the only O(1) possibility. A string is bytes; rune boundaries are only discoverable by walking from the start. s[i] answers 'what byte is at position i' — always O(1), always a uint8:

```go
s := "héllo"
s[0]   // 104 — 'h'
s[1]   // 195 — first byte of é's TWO-byte encoding
s[2]   // 169 — second byte — meaningless as a 'character'
```

Executed. s[1] and s[2] are halves of one rune — blind indexing can hand you a byte that isn't a character at all.

Getting a rune, with the cost stated:

```go
r := []rune(s)[1]   // 233 — é, after an O(n) conversion
```

[]rune(s) decodes the whole string once into an int32 slice — then indexing is O(1). For one-off lookups it's the tool; in a loop it's a per-iteration allocation (range decodes for free).

The design defense: Go chose the cheap honest primitive (byte access, O(1)) over the expensive convenient one (rune access, O(n) hidden behind s[i]). Character logic is opt-in; byte logic is free. ASCII-only programs never pay; Unicode programs say so out loud.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    IDX[s i] --> Q[which byte at position i]
    R[rune s i] --> Q2[which rune at index i]
    IDX --> O[O1 - always a uint8]
    R --> O2[On decode then O1]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why random rune access can't be O(1): UTF-8 code points are variable width, so rune #k's position depends on total widths of runes #0..#k-1 — unknowable without walking. A 'rune index' would either hide an O(n) walk behind s[i] (surprising) or need a parallel index per string (bloating the two-word header). Go chose honest bytes.

The contrast with fixed-width indexing: Java's char (UTF-16, 2 bytes) gave O(1) indexing — until Unicode outgrew 16 bits and surrogate pairs reintroduced variable width (supplementary characters occupy 2 chars — charAt lies about them; the 'fix' is codePointAt with its own semantics). The lesson: variable width is the truth of Unicode; fixed-width was an approximation that broke. Go's byte index never lies; its rune story (range) was correct from day one.

[]rune as the bridge, mechanically: it materializes the parallel structure (an int32 slice — random rune access, O(1), after the one O(n) conversion). Both access patterns at their true costs, and the conversion is the explicit bridge where you pay for random access.

questions.question: What is the difference between len(s) and utf8.RuneCountInString(s)?
questions.title: compare Rune Vs Byte with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: len(s) = BYTES in the string. utf8.RuneCountInString(s) = RUNES (characters). Same only for pure ASCII. 'héllo': len 6, runes 5.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Rune Vs Byte.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: len(s) = BYTES in the string.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Two counts, two units:

```go
s := "héllo"
len(s)                    // 6 — bytes: h(1) é(2) l(1) l(1) o(1)
utf8.RuneCountInString(s) // 5 — runes: h é l l o
```

Executed. ASCII makes them equal (1 byte per rune); any multibyte content diverges them.

len is the honest capacity of what's stored (the string's header field — O(1), no walking). RuneCountInString decodes the whole string, counting code points — O(n). That cost difference matters in hot paths: len is free, rune-count walks everything.

Which to use, by job: byte-count for capacity/protocol limits (wire format sizes are bytes); rune-count for display width logic (approximately — runes aren't exactly screen columns, but closer than bytes); range for anything that also processes the characters (it counts and works in one pass — no separate count).

The bug pattern: a character-limit validator using len(s) — a 10-character emoji-heavy input fails at ~40 bytes. The fix: RuneCountInString, or validate while ranging (count as you go — one O(n) either way, no double pass).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    LEN[len s = bytes] --> |helo| 6
    RC[utf8.RuneCountInString = runes] --> |helo| 5
    ASCII[ASCII: 1 byte = 1 rune]
    UNI[multibyte: diverge]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The two counters' mechanics: len(s) reads the string header's length field (a stored value — that's WHY it's O(1); the count was paid once, at construction). utf8.RuneCountInString iterates and decodes — it's a loop the standard library wrote for you, with the same self-synchronizing walk range uses.

Why 'rune count = character count' is itself approximate: a code point is not a user-perceived character (a grapheme cluster — what users call a character — can be MULTIPLE code points: é can be e + combining accent (2 runes), skin-tone emoji compose from several runes). Go's rune count counts code points, not graphemes — closer than bytes, still not display columns. For true display width: libraries like rivo/uniseg segment graphemes. Interview honesty: state that rune count is the code-point count and name the grapheme distinction — that's the depth signal.

The three-level summary that frames all the string-counting questions: bytes (storage — len), runes (code points — RuneCountInString), graphemes (user characters — third-party segmenters). Every 'how long is this string' question is really 'which unit do you mean' — and APIs that must be exact specify (wire limits: bytes; UI limits: graphemes).

questions.question: What does []rune(s) do, and when do you actually need it?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Rune Vs Byte
questions.direct_answer: Decodes the whole string into an int32 slice — every rune becomes an element, O(n) allocation. Need it for: random rune access by index, rune-level mutation, or rune-level algorithms. NOT for iteration (range is free).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Rune Vs Byte.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Decodes the whole string into an int32 slice — every rune becomes an element, O(n) allocation. Need it for: random rune access by index, rune-level mutation, or rune-level algorithms. NOT.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
[]rune(s) is the explicit decode — a fresh int32 slice holding every code point:

```go
s := "héllo"
r := []rune(s)       // [104 233 108 108 111] — one element per rune
r[1]                  // 233 — é, direct index
r[1] = 'E'            // mutation works — it's a slice
s2 := string(r)       // "hEllo" — re-encode
```

The costs, always: O(n) decode to build, O(n) allocation for the slice, O(n) re-encode on the way back via string(). It's the bridge you pay for when you need SLICE OPERATIONS on characters.

When you need it — the honest list:
1. Random rune access: r[i] — you want the i-th CHARACTER, repeatedly, without re-walking.
2. Rune-level mutation: r[i] = 'X' — building modified strings by position.
3. Rune-based algorithms: reversing a string's characters (swap r[i], r[len-1-i] — the byte version destroys multibyte runes), palindromes over characters, Caesar ciphers.

When you DON'T (the common waste): iteration — range gives each rune for free. Counting — RuneCountInString walks once without materializing a slice. One lookup — utf8.DecodeRuneInString or one range iteration, no slice.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CONV[rune s] --> |On decode + alloc| SL[int32 slice - random access, mutable]
    SL --> |string r - re-encode| BACK[new string]
    RANGE[range s] --> FREE[per-rune, no alloc]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics: []rune(s) runs the UTF-8 decoder over the string, appending each decoded code point to a growing int32 slice — same walk as range, but materializing the output (range discards each rune after the body). string(r) re-encodes each int32 to its UTF-8 bytes into a fresh string. Both directions are full passes with allocation — the bridge's toll.

Why the reverse-a-string idiom REQUIRES []rune — the classic demonstration: swapping bytes of "héllo" by index swaps the HALVES of é (195 and 169 become 169 and 195 — an invalid rune); the result isn't 'olléh' — it's corrupted bytes that decode to replacement characters. Swapping []rune elements moves the whole code point (233) as a unit — correct. Byte-reversal is only safe for known-ASCII inputs, and 'known-ASCII' is the assumption Unicode inputs violate.

The allocation profile interviewers care about: []rune in a LOOP is the same anti-pattern as string↔[]byte in a loop — each conversion allocates. The batch pattern: convert once, operate on the slice, convert back once — mirroring Builder's amortization. The advanced alternative for index-without-materialize: utf8.DecodeRuneInString(s[i:]) walks forward one rune at a time — zero allocation, but you manage the offset arithmetic yourself — the choice between 'readable and allocating' and 'manual and free.'
